evergreen_facts.text: The Oregon Trail carried settlers about 2,000 miles from Missouri to Oregon's Willamette Valley in the 1800s.
Portland, Oregon, got its name from an 1845 coin toss between two founders, one from Maine and one from Boston.
Oregon was admitted to the Union as the 33rd US state on 14 February 1859, Valentine's Day.
Lewis and Clark spent the winter of 1805 to 1806 at Fort Clatsop, near the mouth of the Columbia River in Oregon.
Portland, Oregon, sits where the Willamette River flows into the Columbia River.
The Columbia River forms most of the border between Oregon and Washington state.
Oregon's Crater Lake fills the caldera of Mount Mazama, a volcano that collapsed about 7,700 years ago.
Mount Hood, a snow-capped volcano visible from Portland, is the highest mountain in Oregon.
Multnomah Falls drops in two tiers down the cliffs of the Columbia River Gorge, east of Portland, Oregon.
The Portland Japanese Garden, opened in 1967 in Washington Park, is a traditional garden in Portland, Oregon.
Powell's City of Books in Portland, Oregon, is a bookstore that fills an entire city block.
Mill Ends Park in Portland, Oregon, is a tiny park just two feet across, set in the median of a busy street.
Portland, Oregon, is nicknamed the City of Roses and is home to the International Rose Test Garden.
The marionberry, a blackberry variety bred in Oregon, is named after the state's Marion County.
Tillamook County on the Oregon coast is known for the cheese made by its dairy farmers' cooperative.
The Portland Trail Blazers basketball team won the NBA championship in 1977.
